processing: The historical tea was a steamed green cake, not a modern dark tea, and the exact method is not recorded in detail. Modern teas using the name are recreations, and methods differ by maker.
harvest_season: Not recorded for the historical tea. For a modern product, ask the maker.
appearance_dry: Recorded as thin pieces, light enough that eighty made up one jin.
appearance_liquor: Not recorded for the old tea; modern versions sold as Anhua dark tea would be orange-yellow, as is usual there.
appearance_wet: Not recorded for the old tea; expect dark brown leaf from modern dark tea versions.
taste_profile: No reliable account of the original taste survives. Modern versions sold as Anhua dark tea can be expected to taste mellow and lightly woody, typical of the region.

brewing.notes: For a modern dark tea version, use the usual Anhua method: a quick rinse and boiling water. Follow the maker's advice if the tea is made differently.

vintage_note: The original tea is long gone, so there is no continuous vintage tradition. What sells today is a modern product under an old name, usually carrying a production year. Judge it by its maker and date, not by the Tang story on the box.
description:
Qujiang Bo Pian, the thin slices of Qujiang, is the earliest named tea tied to Anhua. It takes its name from Qujiang, a town on a bend of the Zi River, and it is remembered through old texts rather than through any tea you can trace in an unbroken line.

It was a steamed cake tea, thin enough that eighty pieces weighed one jin. That makes it a relative of Tang and Five Dynasties green cakes, not of the fermented, pine-smoked tea Anhua is known for now. Listing it among dark teas reflects its place in Anhua's story, and modern products, more than its original character.

Nothing reliable tells us how it tasted. A modern tea under this name should be treated as a new tea: brew it as the maker suggests and judge it on its own terms.

When buying, be wary of claims that a tea follows the Tang recipe, because the old method is not recorded in that detail.
history:
The Tang writer Yang Ye mentions the tea in Shanfu Jingshou Lu, the earliest text to record Anhua tea, and says it travelled to Jiangling, Xiangyang and on to Chang'an. Mao Wenxi's Cha Pu, from the Five Dynasties, gives the often-quoted figure of eighty pieces to the jin.

It was one of several named Hunan teas of the Tang. Anhua's move toward pan-firing, piling and fire-drying came later, from the Ming, and little is known of how or when the old slices stopped being made.
sources_note: History is backed by press citations of the old texts, not the texts themselves. Modern product details are thin.
